1:
Both of the close readers notice that this is Mark's scene and nobody else's. Ellicott points out that where the other account says only that the disciples came to show him the buildings, Mark gives the man's very words; Robertson says the same and adds a guess at the speaker, that it may have been Peter, trying by a pleasant platitude to turn the Teacher's mind away from the grim subjects of the last few hours in the temple. It was not a new observation. The merest commonplace, Robertson says, might serve at such a crisis.

The stones themselves are described from two sources that do not quite agree. Barnes and Clarke both quote Josephus, who reports white marble blocks fifty feet long, twenty-four broad and sixteen thick, a scale Clarke thinks enough by itself to account for the disciples' wonder. Robertson prefers what can still be measured: stones surviving at the south-eastern and south-western angles run from twenty to forty feet long and weigh a hundred tons apiece.

Why the man said it divides the commentators. Henry takes it as a symptom: how apt Christ's own disciples are to idolize what looks great and has long been counted sacred. They had just heard him call the place a den of thieves, and now they court him to admire its stonework, as if pleading with him not to leave so fine a place. Ellicott is gentler, calling it the natural admiration of Galilean peasants, but makes the same charge in the end: fresh from the lesson of the poor widow they were still measuring things by quantity and size, and admired the goodly stones more than the mite. Bede sets the two scenes in a deliberate order, the Lord praising the devotedness of the Church in the person of the widow and then going out to foretell the ruin of the building.

On the answer Henry draws the contrast he wants: Christ looks with pity on the ruin of precious souls and weeps over them, but shows no such concern for the ruin of a magnificent house. He notices too where the temple's strength lay, in the sheer size of the stones, so that if these are thrown down no footstep and no remembrance of it remains — while any part stood there might be hope of repair, but none once no stone is left on another. Robertson observes that Jesus grants the greatness and beauty without argument, which is what makes the demolition remarkable; the verb, he says, means loosened down, and only the foundation stones remain.

That last point is exactly where an objection was raised, and Theophylact meets it head on. Some, he reports, try to prove the words false by pointing out that many ruins were left standing. His first answer is that this misses the point, since at the consummation of all things not one stone shall be left upon another; his second is historical, that Aelius Hadrian overturned the city and the temple from their foundations, and so the word spoken here was fulfilled.

Two of the older readers look past the masonry. Bede argues that the removal was ordered by divine power: once the grace of the gospel was known through the world, the temple and its ceremonies had to be taken away, lest someone weak in faith, seeing institutions of God's own appointing still standing, should slip by degrees back into a carnal Judaism. He adds that when the Lord left the building, the whole edifice of the law went with it, and that with the head taken away the limbs fight one against another. Pseudo-Jerome reads the stones themselves as testimonies of the prophets, not one of which would be left standing upon the men to whom the Jews had perversely applied them, on Ezra, on Zerubbabel, on the Maccabees.
3:
The place where the question was asked gets more attention than one might expect. Barnes states the geography plainly, the Mount of Olives directly east of the city with a fine view of the temple from it. Ellicott adds that Mark alone mentions the vantage point, and that the view it commanded makes everything that follows more vivid; he thinks it may have been at or near the very spot where, a few days before, Jesus had paused and wept over the city. Bede alone makes the posture itself speak. The Lord sits on the mount opposite the temple while he discourses on its ruin, so that even his bodily position agrees with his words, showing mystically that he abides in peace with the saints and hates the madness of the proud — for the mount of olives, Bede says, marks the fruitful sublimity of the Church.

Lightfoot recovers a detail of temple practice that the phrase over against recalls. The east wall of the court of the Gentiles was kept low, unlike the others, because the priest who burned the red heifer stood on the top of Olivet and had to sight the temple gate across it; he killed the heifer with his right hand, took the blood in his left, and sprinkled it with his right seven times straight toward the holy of holies. The temple could be seen from any part of the ridge, but the words over against point to that line, and Lightfoot cannot help remembering the priest's action there.

Who asked is also noticed. Ellicott lists three things about the four names: that Mark alone gives them; that this is the only occasion on which Andrew is joined to the three who elsewhere form the inner circle; and that Andrew, though the first called, stands last in the list.

What they were asking about is the real difficulty, and the witnesses answer it four ways. Wesley finds two distinct questions here, one about the destruction of the city and one about the end of the world. Ellicott hears something subtler in the wording: Mark uses vaguer terms where the parallel has the definite sign of thy coming and of the end of the world, which he suggests may be characteristic of a Gospel written for Gentiles. Augustine will not separate the strands at all, taking the reply to cover things that were to have their course from that time forward — the destruction of Jerusalem that prompted the question, the Lord's own coming through the Church, in which he comes continually since his members are born day by day, and the end itself when he appears to judge the living and the dead. Robertson reaches a similar position by a different road. He reports the modern theory that treats this chapter as a Jewish apocalypse adapted and put in Jesus' mouth, and prefers the view that Jesus blended in one picture his own death, the fall of the city within that generation, and the second coming which that fall typifies; the lines between the topics, he grants, are not sharply drawn.

Cyril of Jerusalem takes the question as a model of how to ask it. The things that are seen shall pass away and better things come, but as to the time let no one be curious, since it is not for us to know the times the Father has kept in his own power. His warning runs in both directions at once: do not venture to declare when these things shall be, and do not on that account supinely slumber. The signs of the end had to be known, he argues, precisely so that we should not die deceived by a false Christ, and it was under that necessity that the apostles put their question to the true Teacher.
5:
Henry reads the whole answer as a redirection. Christ sets himself not to satisfy their curiosity but to direct their consciences, leaving the times and seasons where the Father has kept them and giving instead the cautions they would actually need. The first is against being deceived: having found the true Messiah, do not lose him again in the crowd of pretenders. Henry notes the historical shape of it, that only after the true Christ was rejected were the people imposed upon by false ones, never before, and adds that when many are deceived we should be awakened to look to ourselves.

Who the deceivers were is answered from three periods. Bede names the men who came forward while destruction hung over the city, claiming to be Christs, and adds that teachers of heresy arose inside the Church in the apostles' own time, the first of the antichrists being Simon Magus, whom the Samaritans called the great power of God. Cyril of Jerusalem reckons the prediction fulfilled only in part, naming Simon and Menander among the godless leaders of heresy and expecting others in his own day or after him. Robertson brings the charge to the present: in every age men have tried to fit this picture to the calamity of their own time. On the wording, Clarke reports that a number of manuscripts and several old versions add the title, making it I am the Christ, while Ellicott takes the plain Greek to be simply I am He and treats Christ as a necessary inference from the context.

The wars are read at two levels. Theophylact makes them the Romans against the Jews, and draws on Josephus for the sequence: when the Jews refused tribute the Romans rose in anger, but being at that time merciful took their spoils without destroying the city — and what follows, he says, shows that God himself was fighting against them. Robertson documents the period rather than interpreting it: outbreaks at Alexandria, at Seleucia with more than fifty thousand killed, at Jamnia; four famines under Claudius, one in Judaea; and earthquakes in Crete, at Rome, in Phrygia and in Campania before the city fell. Bede alone turns the phrase inward, suggesting that kingdom against kingdom may rather be understood of heretics, who by fighting one another bring about the triumph of the Church. He also fixes what the disciples were not to conclude: the end was not to come at once, but was put off some forty years, and meanwhile they were not to abandon Jerusalem in fear.

Henry builds his second caution on exactly that point, and gives four reasons for not being troubled. The wars should be no surprise, since they were foretold and serve God's purposes; no terror, because those who do not covet the smiles of the world need not dread its frowns; no omen that the world is ending, since other counsels stand between; and no proof that God has done his worst, for he has more arrows in his quiver. The result Henry claims is a holy security of mind while everything around is in disorder.

On the closing phrase Barnes supplies the image the English hides, that the word means the pains of a woman in travail, while Clarke notes that many copies have the singular, the beginning. Lightfoot shows what the phrase would have stirred in the hearers, since the scribes had taught the nation to expect Gog and Magog immediately before the Messiah, one rabbi saying that when you see the kingdoms disturbing one another you may expect the footsteps of the Messiah. Cyril of Jerusalem, reading the same signs, asks his hearers directly whether there is not war at that moment between Persians and Romans, and answers his own question: these things have already come to pass.
9:
Ellicott notices two things before reading the block. The emphatic repetition of the warning is peculiar to Mark, who sounds it again later in the chapter; and the whole description of the disciples' sufferings stands here where the parallel discourse in the other Gospel does not have it, its material appearing instead in the earlier commission to the Twelve.

What the warning asks for is read narrowly and broadly. Gill takes it to concern not their doctrine or conversation, as the phrase sometimes does, but the security of their persons: they were to avoid falling into the hands of persecutors wherever it could honestly be avoided. Barnes allows both senses, against deception and against unnecessary danger alike.

The tribunals named are sorted out with some precision. Clarke distinguishes the ranks: the great Sanhedrin of seventy-two elders, six from each tribe, the lesser Sanhedrins of twenty-three, the synagogue courts of three magistrates that served the villages, the governors who were Roman deputies like Pilate, and the kings who were the tetrarchs of the two provinces. Robertson adds that the word for council is the name of the body at Jerusalem, the local ones modelled on it, and recovers the force of the verb rendered beaten: it properly means to flay or skin, softened in common speech as our own words for a beating are.

Over one phrase the witnesses divide. Barnes insists that for a testimony against them should rather be to them: the disciples were to stand as witnesses of the truth before their judges. Theophylact reads it as a sentence rather than a witness — a judgment given beforehand, so that men who would not join themselves to the truth while the apostles laboured for it might be left inexcusable.

The promise of the Spirit draws the fullest treatment. The Gloss supplies the anxiety it answers: brought before kings, the disciples might fear their want of learning and eloquence would leave them speechless. Barnes takes the promise at its strongest, as a pledge of inspiration, so that the defences recorded afterwards are the words of the Holy Ghost himself. Robertson accepts the promise but fences it: Jesus is speaking of defences before councils and governors, not of preaching, and there is no excuse here for the lazy preacher who leaves his sermon unprepared on a mistaken reliance upon the Spirit. Calvin holds the same balance from the other side. The design is to relieve the disciples of the anxiety that interferes with a cheerful discharge of duty, yet not to let them fall asleep in indolent security; what is promised, he adds from the parallel wording, is not deliverance from death, which must not always be expected, but the confounding of their adversaries.

On the gospel going first to all nations the interest is textual and historical. Clarke reports that many of the lectionaries omit the verse altogether and thinks its proper place is later in the passage; Robertson notes that the clause is Mark's alone and that Paul could already claim the gospel had spread over the world, all of it before the city fell.

Bede and Theophylact close the section by explaining why it was said at all. Bede holds that the greatest cause of the nation's destruction was that after killing the Saviour they tormented the heralds of his name, and that the Lord, knowing his disciples would be saddened by their country's fall, consoled them with the promise that far more would be gathered out of all mankind than perished in Judaea. Theophylact says he set out the apostles' own troubles first so that they might take comfort in the company of sufferers, and that forewarning of betrayal by their own families would help them bear it. His summary of the matter is the line that has outlived him: it is not the punishment but the cause that makes the martyr.
14:
What the abomination of desolation is gets five answers. Gill and Henry both take it for the Roman army encircling the city — a thing abominable to the Jews and desolating to their nation, city and temple. Henry sharpens that into an exchange: they had rejected Christ as an abomination, who would have been their salvation, and God gave them an abomination that was their desolation. Theophylact says much the same more briefly, calling it the violent entry of enemies into the city. Bede will not settle on one thing. It may be said simply of Antichrist, or of the statue of Caesar that Pilate set up in the temple, or of the equestrian statue of Hadrian which stood for a long time in the holy of holies itself; an idol is called an abomination in the older scriptures, and of desolation because it was placed in a temple already desolate and deserted. Augustine works instead on the wording, showing that where it ought not and the other Gospel's in the holy place say the same thing, and that the third account fixes the moment by defining it as the city compassed with armies.

Robertson brings a parallel none of the others has. The exact phrase in the first Gospel is the one used in the Maccabean history of the altar to Zeus that Antiochus Epiphanes raised where the altar to the Lord had stood; Mark, however, treats the abomination as a person, using a masculine participle, while the third Gospel defines it by the armies. So the prophet's words find a second fulfilment, with Rome standing where Syria had stood. On the parenthesis that follows, Clarke notes only that one manuscript and three of the old Latin copies fill it out to let him that readeth understand what he readeth, which he thinks needless. Wesley glosses the phrase where it ought not in five words: that place being set apart for sacred use. Bede takes the same parenthesis as an instruction about method — when we are challenged to understand what is said, we may conclude that the saying is mystical.

Henry presses the affront rather than the identification. The army stood where it ought not, in and about the holy city, which the heathen ought never to have approached and would not have been suffered to approach had Jerusalem not first profaned the crown of its own holiness.

That the flight was actually made is Bede's contribution, and he gives it as history. On the approach of the war with Rome, all the Christians in the province, warned by this prophecy, fled far away, crossed the Jordan and settled for a time at Pella under the protection of Agrippa, who with the Jews that obeyed him remained subject to the empire. Theophylact adds a detail that limits the warning's audience: the words name those who are in Judaea, and the Apostles were no longer there, having been driven out of Jerusalem before the fighting began.

The manner of the flight is read at two levels. The Gloss keeps it literal and urgent, working through what would hold a man back — the desire to carry away property from the house, children to be carried, and the season — and states the principle plainly, that it is a desirable thing to be saved even naked from such a destruction. Pseudo-Jerome turns the whole scene inward: our flight is to the mountains, so that he who has climbed to the heights of virtue may not go down again to the depths of sin. Even the prayer about the season he reads that way, taking winter and sabbath as the ending of fruit and the ending of time, so that what is asked is that the fruit of our work should not be cut off when time itself runs out.
17:
The two hindrances named first are read literally and then darkly. Gill takes the woe to women with child and nursing mothers at face value: their burden makes them unfit for haste and so likely to fall into the enemy's hands. Theophylact hears something worse in the phrase and says so — it seems to him that the words foretell the eating of children, since when famine and pestilence came the people laid hands on their own.

On the prayer about the season the interest divides between the practical and the textual. Gill lists what winter would mean for fugitives: short days, bad roads, inclement weather, and mountains that are wretched lodging. Ellicott points instead at what Mark leaves out. The clause nor on the sabbath day, prominent in the parallel report, is absent here, and he takes the omission as characteristic of a Gospel written for Gentile readers — a reader outside Judaism would not feel the difficulty.

The tribulation itself is where the chapter's largest question opens, and the witnesses stand in three places. Gill keeps it to the siege: the fury of the zealots, the sword within and without, and the plagues and famines. Theophylact reads the shortening the same way and draws out its logic: had the Roman war not been finished quickly no Jew would have escaped, and it was for the sake of the believing Jews, and of those who would believe afterwards, that God cut the days short, foreseeing that many would come to faith after the city fell and so refusing to let the whole race be destroyed.

Bede and Cyril of Jerusalem move the passage forward instead. Bede holds that the words about affliction properly agree with the times of Antichrist, when not only will torments be more frequent and more painful than before but — what he calls more terrible still — the working of miracles will accompany those who inflict them; and he sets the length at three years and a half, the tribulation being shorter in proportion as it is greater. Cyril reaches the same span by the same prophet and is careful about his authority for it, insisting that he speaks not from apocryphal books but from Daniel. His pastoral conclusion is unusual: let those who know themselves stout-hearted enough to face the adversary stand, for he does not despair of the Church's nerve, and let those of us who are fearful provide for our own safety.

Augustine tries to hold both readings at once and has to qualify the text to do it. He grants that in the time of Antichrist there will be a tribulation equal or greater, and saves the words never shall be by restricting them to that people: if the Jews are the first to receive Antichrist, they may then be said to cause the tribulation rather than to suffer it. He also reports a reading of the shortening that he thinks fitter than the arithmetical one — that the days stand for the calamities done in them, as scripture elsewhere calls days evil though the days themselves are not; and on that reading the woes were abridged because the patience God gave made them felt less, so that what was great in itself was cut down.

Wesley, alone, refuses to close the question. May it not be doubted, he asks, whether this has yet been fully accomplished, and whether much of the affliction is not still to come. On the elect for whose sake the days are shortened they are the Christians, taken out of the world through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth, and he shortened means he will surely shorten. Robertson notes that the clause naming them as those whom he chose stands in Mark alone and rests the end of the whole matter on the sovereign choice of God.
21:
The first question is what then means, and Theophylact will not let it be read as a sequence. Having finished with Jerusalem, the Lord now speaks of the coming of Antichrist; but the word does not mean immediately upon the city's fall. Theophylact takes his parallel from the other evangelist, who writes that in those days came John the Baptist without meaning the days just after the nativity. The word is used indefinitely and without precision, and here it points not to the desolation of Jerusalem but to the time of Antichrist.

Bede argues the same conclusion from the circumstances instead. Some, he reports, refer the warning to the Jewish war, when many declaring themselves Christs drew crowds of deluded people after them; but during the siege there was no Christian in the city to whom an exhortation against following false teachers could apply. He prefers to understand it of heretics who came against the Church pretending to be Christs, the first of them Simon Magus and the last and greatest Antichrist. Gill, who takes the plainer view throughout, simply records that false Christs and false prophets arose both before and after the destruction of the city.

Augustine opens a question about the wonders themselves and declines to close it. Satan will be unchained and will work through Antichrist in all his power, wonderfully but falsely; and it is often asked whether the apostolic phrase about lying wonders means that he deceives the senses with phantoms, appearing to do what he does not, or that the wonders are genuine and are lying only in their effect, because men who do not know the reach of Satan's power will not believe that anything but God could do them. Augustine leaves both readings standing and settles the matter on other ground: whichever is meant, those will be deceived by such signs who deserve to be deceived. He also says why the woes were foretold at all — that having the troubles announced beforehand, and then feeling them, we might look for our reward at the end with more confidence.

Gregory takes up the hardest phrase in the sentence. Why is it said with a doubt, if it were possible, when the Lord knows beforehand what will be? His answer turns the conditional into a definition: if they are elect it is not possible, and if it is possible they are not elect. The hesitation in the words, he says, is not the Lord's uncertainty but the trembling in the mind of the elect themselves, who are called elect because he sees that they will persevere in faith and good works, and who are for that very reason the ones the preachers of Antichrist will try hardest to shake.

Gill reaches the same balance from the Reformed side and states both halves of it. The purposes of God concerning the salvation of his elect cannot be frustrated, his promises are yea and amen, his grace efficacious, his power uncontrollable, and the salvation of the chosen certain; and it still becomes them to be on their guard against every deception and to use all the means of perseverance.

Robertson notices that the two accounts do not quite agree on the grammar of the seduction: Mark's construction expresses purpose, a view to leading the elect away, where the parallel expresses result. On the closing warning he is blunt in his own voice. Gullibility is no mark of a saint or of piety, credulity ranks no higher than scepticism, God gave us our wits for self-protection, and Christ has warned us beforehand. Ellicott adds the observation that ties the section back to the earlier one: the repeated warning word here, as before, is peculiar to Mark.
24:
Henry treats these verses as the correction of the disciples' whole mistake. They had run the destruction of Jerusalem and the end of the world together, assuming the temple must stand as long as the world; the phrase after that tribulation separates them, putting the judgment later, not alongside. Henry adds the pastoral consequence: those who lived to see the nation destroyed were not to conclude, because the Son of man did not visibly come in the clouds then, that he never would. Wesley reads the days as those immediately preceding the end of the world.

Gill goes the other way entirely and reads the whole passage of the first century. The stars that fall are the rabbins and doctors who fell away from the written word and compiled the oral law. The seeing of the Son of man is not in person but in the power of his wrath, of which those Jews had convincing proof. And the angels sent out are the ministers of the gospel, sent to preach and plant more churches among the Gentiles now that the church at Jerusalem was broken up.

The darkened lights draw the widest range of readings. Robertson warns against pressing them: the figures are drawn from the prophets, apocalyptic imagery was not always meant to be taken literally, and Peter applied the very prophecy about sun and moon to the day of Pentecost. Bede and Theophylact agree on a cause that keeps the lights intact — they are outshone, obscured not by any loss of their own light but by the brightness of the true Light — though Bede allows that the bodies may really lose their light for a time, as the sun did at the Passion. Theophylact reads the falling stars as the angelic powers themselves, astonished at such great things done and at the judging of their fellow-servants. Pseudo-Jerome takes every term morally: the sun darkened at the coldness of men's hearts as in winter, the moon losing her serenity in a time of quarrel, the stars failing when the seed of Abraham to which they were likened has all but disappeared.

Who sees what, and in what form, is Augustine's concern. Since the angels said he would come in the same manner as he was seen to go, we rightly believe he will come not only in the same body but on a cloud. The vision of the Son of man is granted even to the wicked, while the vision of the form of God belongs to the pure in heart alone; and because both just and unjust must see their Judge, it was necessary that the Son of man should receive the power to judge. Ellicott points at the wording rather than the doctrine: Mark's plain they shall see the Son of man both replaces and explains the sign of the Son of man in the parallel. Cyril of Jerusalem, reading that parallel, builds the sign into a scene: Christ's own true sign is the Cross, and a luminous cross shall go before the King, declaring plainly the one who was crucified, so that the sign is terror to his foes and joy to his friends.

The gathering is described in details Mark alone preserves or omits. Ellicott notes the absence of the trumpet that is prominent in the other account, and Robertson remarks how brief the Greek is — from the tip of earth to the tip of heaven, a phrase occurring nowhere else. Bede guards it against a narrow reading: the four winds are the four quarters of the world, and the further phrase is added lest anyone suppose the elect are gathered only from the edges. Theophylact draws a conclusion from the sending itself, that Christ despatches the angels as the Father does, and asks where then are they who say he is not equal to the Father.
28:
Gill sets the parable in its place before anyone allegorizes it. They were sitting on the Mount of Olives, where fig trees grew in great plenty, so one may well have been in view; and the passover being at hand, it was exactly the season for the tree to put forth.

The older readers take the tree further. Bede makes it the synagogue, condemned to barrenness for having no fruits of righteousness when the Lord came; but since the Apostle promised that when the fulness of the Gentiles is come in all Israel shall be saved, the long-barren tree will yet yield the fruit it has withheld, and when that happens a summer of true peace is at hand. Theophylact reads the speed of it rather than the tree: as leaves are followed at once by summer, so the woes of Antichrist will be followed by the coming of Christ without an interval — summer after winter to the just, and to sinners winter after summer.

Ellicott raises a textual question that reaches past the verse. Many of the best manuscripts read it is known rather than ye know; he takes that for an early copyist's slip — and, notably, a slip in the document he supposes underlies all three reports, since the parallels agree against it.

What this generation means is the hardest question in the chapter, and five answers stand side by side. Gill takes it strictly of the men then living, ruling out mankind in general, the Jews as a people, and Christians. Henry agrees and adds the arithmetic of it: the disciples themselves were taken away from the evil to come, all but one, while the generation they trained up lived to see it. Clarke argues for a second sense of the word, this very race of men, conceding first that it can mean a fixed term — Moses uses it of a period of thirty-eight years, which is precisely the interval between this prediction and the destruction of the city — but preferring the other because events in the chapter plainly look beyond that destruction and were to fall out before the Jews ceased to be a distinct people. Theophylact excludes the apostles, since most did not live to see the city fall, and makes it the generation of Christians, to console the disciples lest they think the faith would fail. Bede leaves it open between the whole race of mankind and the Jews in particular. Wesley cuts the knot from the other end by narrowing what is promised rather than who is addressed: all these things means the things relating to the temple and the city.

Augustine stands apart from all of them. Comparing the three accounts closely, he thinks nearly everything in them may belong to the Lord's daily coming in his body, the Church, except where the last coming is unmistakably named; so that when these things are seen the end is not yet, but near at hand. Even the gathering of the elect from the four winds he reads that way — a collecting that goes on throughout the whole of the last hour, the Lord coming in his members as in clouds.

On the passing of heaven and earth the question is how much passes. Bede restricts it: the heaven that passes is not the starry heaven but the region of the air, since the fire of judgment will reach wherever the water of the earlier judgment reached; and heaven and earth pass in the form they now have while lasting without end in their essence. Gill allows the words either as a statement of what will happen at the second coming or as a comparison, meaning that the frame of the world will go sooner than anything Christ has said. Theophylact takes the second sense outright: the immoveable elements fail before the words of Christ do.
32:
This verse gives the chapter its sharpest difficulty, and the witnesses divide before reaching it. Gill takes the day and the hour to be those of Jerusalem's destruction, on the ground that Christ had been speaking of nothing else and the words look back to what precedes. Robertson holds the opposite and gives a reason: the disclaimer of knowledge naturally applies to the second coming, since the fall of the city had just been fixed within that generation, as in fact it did. Wesley sides with him on usage: that day is scripture's emphatic name for the judgment.

Whether the clause about the Son belongs in the text at all is the next question. Clarke reports from Ambrose that it was wanting in some Greek copies, notes that it appears in neither of the parallel accounts, and says he strongly suspects it was not originally in this Gospel. Barnes answers that the words are now found in all the manuscripts; Robertson is more definite still, saying there is no doubt here of the kind that exists over the parallel passage.

Granting the words, what they can mean is disputed by every school at once. Barnes reports and dismisses one evasion, that the verb means to make known, so that the sense would be that none makes that day known — which only prompts the question where and when the Father made it known. His own answer is the two natures: the difficulty is no greater than in the statement that Jesus increased in wisdom and stature; he had a human nature, grew as a man in knowledge, and as a man his knowledge must be finite. Clarke finds that hard to accept. He confesses it utterly unaccountable that one who foretold these events to a jot and tittle, in whom the fulness of the Godhead dwelt bodily, should not know this, and can account for it only by supposing that the Deity dwelling in the man Christ Jesus communicated less knowledge of the future at one time than at another.

Hilary refuses the terms of the question altogether. He asks whether it is credible that the cause of all things that are and are to be should be ignorant of any of them, or that the Lord of glory should not know the day of his own coming. He then presses the other side of it: to say the Father withheld this is to ascribe envy to him, since he gave the Son foreknowledge of his own death. His resolution is verbal rather than metaphysical: all the treasures of wisdom are in him, and scripture says they are hidden in him, so the ignorance must be the hiding of those treasures, not their absence.

Theophylact answers pastorally, and makes two observations the others miss. Had the Lord said I know but will not tell you, he would have saddened them considerably; by naming the angels and himself he stopped the question without wounding them. And the words as they stand, Theophylact points out, do not say I do not know when the time will be, but ye know not. Why it was concealed he thinks was mercy: if we are careless while we do not know the end, what should we do if we knew — keep on in our wickedness until it came.

Gill makes the concealment itself the reason for the command that follows: the day was withheld so that Christ's people might be on guard against false Christs, and might watch unto prayer, lest the day come upon them unawares. Ellicott, noting the characteristic repetition of the warning word, adds an observation reaching past this verse. The three Gospels agree closely up to this point and then conclude the discourse quite differently, as though they had rested on a common document which stopped here and left each to his own memory or tradition.
34:
The parable's frame is read the same way by nearly everyone. Bede identifies the man who went abroad as Christ, ascending as a conqueror to his Father after the Resurrection, leaving his Church as to his bodily presence but never depriving her of the safeguard of his divine presence. Gregory locates the journey: earth is properly the place of flesh, and that flesh was carried into a far country when the Redeemer set it in the heavens.

Who the porter is gets three answers of widening scope. Barnes keeps it literal: the door-keeper who attends those who come and go. Clarke makes it the ministers of the Gospel, who should continually watch for the safety and welfare of the whole flock. Gregory agrees that the porter is the order of pastors, commanded to have a care over the Church committed to them, but immediately widens it: not only those who rule over churches, but every one of us is required to watch the doors of his own heart, lest the evil suggestions of the devil get in.

Ellicott, alone, finds the parable puzzling rather than plain. He observes that the words that make the opening sentence work are supplied by the translators and absent from the Greek, and calls their absence singular. His explanation is that this may be an imperfect, fragmentary report — a note taken at the time — of what appears developed elsewhere as the parable of the talents; and he hears the closing warning about being found asleep as a similar reminiscence of the wise and foolish virgins.

The four watches are named and then read at two levels. Barnes and Robertson identify them as the four divisions of the night, and Ellicott fixes the hours at nine, midnight, three and six. Ellicott also makes something of the vagueness: these words left on Peter's mind, and were meant to leave, the impression that the promise of his Lord's coming was undefined as to times and seasons. Theophylact turns the same four watches into the span of one life — evening is dying in old age, midnight dying in the midst of youth, and cockcrow the age when reason comes to its strength, for when a child begins to live by his reason the cock cries loud within him and rouses him out of the sleep of sense.

The warning is about one's own death as much as the end, and Augustine and Pseudo-Jerome press it hardest. Augustine begins from the audience: the Lord speaks not only to those then hearing but to all who came after, to us, and to all who follow, until his last coming — and since that day will not find all men living, the command must reach each man by another route, namely his own end. That day comes to each when his day comes for departing this life, in the state he will be in when judged; so the man whom the last day of his life finds unprepared is the man the Advent will find unprepared. Pseudo-Jerome argues the same by comparison: a sleeper's mind is on phantoms, and when he wakes he possesses nothing of what he saw — which is what happens to those whom the love of this world seizes, who leave at death what they dreamed was solid.

The closing words widen the audience beyond the four who asked. Gill notes the discourse was given privately to Peter, James, John and Andrew, and Pseudo-Jerome that the Lord ends by making the last hear from the first a precept common to all. Clarke's version is a question: does a prisoner expecting his deliverance need to be told to hold himself in readiness to leave his dungeon? And Ellicott closes with evidence of how deeply the command took hold: the Christian names that mean watchful, Gregory and Vigilius among them.
